claims.text: The initial materials are multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles.
Conventional cooling produces a moderate density of synthesis-induced defects in these nanoparticles.
Reducing synthesis-induced defect density enhances intrinsic compositional uniformity.
Greater intrinsic compositional uniformity improves retention of a single-phase solid solution and chemical homogeneity during high-temperature service.
Faster cooling rates reduce lattice-defect density.
Optimized post-synthesis annealing reduces lattice-defect density.
Optimized post-synthesis annealing promotes compositional homogeneity.
Lattice-defect density controls nanoscale compositional uniformity.
Lower defect density reduces local energy variations.
Defect-associated local energy variations act as nucleation sites for phase segregation or precipitation.
Suppressing such nucleation sites minimizes thermally activated decomposition and preserves chemical homogeneity.
After high-temperature exposure, defect-minimized nanoparticles will contain fewer secondary phases than conventionally prepared nanoparticles.
After high-temperature exposure, defect-minimized nanoparticles will exhibit less compositional inhomogeneity and microstructural degradation than the baseline.
Baseline nanoparticles with moderate defect densities have a higher propensity for phase segregation or precipitation under service conditions.
Composition and annealing temperature can affect phase decomposition and its characteristic length scale in high-entropy alloys.
Bulk alloys and systems containing engineered nanoprecipitates may exhibit stability behavior different from the proposed nanoparticle mechanism.
The defect-density threshold needed to suppress segregation and the magnitude of the resulting stability improvement are unknown.
